Y is higher than X - Anthropic and Open AI have more leverage over the infrastructure/cloud providers.

For a given token over time all else equal, the cloud and infrastructure players charge more for open source tokens vs. what Anthropic and OpenAI pay per token b/c open source has no leverage.

The difference you are seeing in pricing is the function of margins at the model layer (which are stacked on top the prices that the cloud providers charge per token). The model layer earns a much higher margin when it is a closed, frontier token vs. much lower margins when it is an open source token.

The infrastructure layer charges more per token for open source tokens all else equal over time.

Current scarcity dynamics and the insane rates at which Anthropic and OpenAI can monetize a gigawatt (100b) are letting them pay more for tokens to maximize revenue. Once we are past compute scarcity, whenever that may be, everything normalizes and revenues to the infrastructure layer are higher for open source tokens than frontier tokens.

Ranges make sense but you've got to think hard about how much risk you want to allocate to the alpha (your views) vs. the beta (just being long a diversified set of assets).  As you say, rebalancing is one of the hardest things in a long-term savings portfolio.

For many investors easier to hold a diversified asset core allocation (say 60/40, or risk parity or whatever you like) which does asset rebalancing for you without thought (or tax consequences) and explicitly allocate capital to your alpha bucket that you play with.  Sometimes even better in a totally different account so you dont overallocate to it.

Investing is a head game more than anything.

Tokenized assets were central to Avalanche’s early institutional story, but the network’s role now reaches well beyond issuance.

OpenTrade distributes tokenized yield products through fintechs and exchanges across Latin America and Europe. Its Avalanche-based vaults have grown to more than $190 million in TVL.

Avalanche is now being used for much more than issuing tokenized assets.

$MRNA The Surprise of the Season

So what really sent $MRNA up 177%, adding roughly $35 billion to its market value?

We honestly cannot remember seeing anything like this in the 30 years we have been in the market.

It is true that the trial was stopped successfully three years ahead of schedule because of strong efficacy, and that is probably worth around $2–3 billion in NPV to $MRNA.

But the Phase 3 results were very similar to what we already saw in Phase 2, so where the hell did the other $32.5 billion of market value come from?

First, the market did not expect the trial to stop early. Usually, Phase 3 trials are designed to confirm the Phase 2 results, and because the Phase 2 and Phase 3 results were so similar, the expectation was that the trial would continue until completion.

The statistical design of the Phase 3 trial was not something $MRNA had shared with the market, so investors could not know in advance that the trial would be stopped early.

The surprise factor therefore added several billion dollars to the valuation.

Another factor behind the move was the major banks and brokers.

As you can see in the table above, almost all the major banks and brokers were Neutral on the stock, except BofA, which had a Sell rating.

This means the banks and brokers were effectively recommending that their clients use the stock as a source of funds, or in other words, short it.

And indeed, short interest in the stock was around 14% of the free float, compared with an average of roughly 5% in the S&P 500.

That means we saw the mother of all short squeezes today.

And it continued after hours, with the stock continuing to climb.

It is also important to mention that the melanoma success made investors more optimistic about the company’s other indications.

Since the Phase 3 results were very similar to the Phase 2 results, this probably should not have happened to this extent.

And last but not least:

One of the major brokers, ranked number two among institutional investors, was forced to explain to its clients that a cure for cancer has still not been discovered.

If professional investors were asking them, “Has a cure for cancer been found?”, imagine what retail investors are thinking.

To sum it up,

This madness will probably end when the short squeeze ends, and then the stock is likely to pull back.

We would not buy at these levels, and we would consider a long-term short, while fully understanding that in the short term the stock can go wherever it wants.

The Bessent Put

Today the US Treasury doubled the size of its long-end bond buybacks, the day after the 30-year yield hit a 19-year high at 5.33%. The extra dollars are small. The signal is enormous.

For the first time, the fiscal authority, not the Fed, stepped in to defend the long end within 24 hours of the highs. There is now a put under the long bond, and the market has just been told the top of the range...

Look at the plumbing underneath it... 

The buybacks pull old, illiquid bonds off dealer balance sheets and get funded at the front end with bills, which the banking system absorbs. Duration out, money-like paper in. Lower long-end volatility raises the collateral value of every Treasury in the repo system, which is itself a liquidity easing. And the QRA language quietly changed two weeks ago to allow exactly this.

This month's joint yen intervention was about stopping Japan from ever becoming a forced seller of Treasuries, and the new dollar swap lines across Asia and the Gulf keep the region's dollar debts rolling, with China the ultimate beneficiary.
